title: Patient safety incident
description: A report of one patient safety event: an incident that reached a patient, a near miss that didn't, or an unsafe condition that could lead to either. It holds the event's classification, the harm assessment, contributing factors, immediate actions, notifications, the investigation and its action plan, and any submission to a patient safety organization. The event types, categories and harm levels follow the concepts of the AHRQ Common Formats for Event Reporting – Hospital and the WHO Conceptual Framework for the International Classification for Patient Safety (ICPS), so reports can be mapped to them; the format is not an implementation of either and is not certified by AHRQ or WHO. It carries as little protected health information as it can: there are no fields for patient names, dates of birth, contact details or record numbers. Records are still not de-identified data (event dates, the facility and free text can identify a patient), so treat every record as confidential.

$schema.title: Schema
$schema.description: The `$id` of the schema the record follows, so a reader can tell what the record is without guessing. Optional; recordType and schemaVersion say the same thing.

recordType.title: Record type
recordType.description: Always patient-safety-incident. Lets a reader (or validate()) tell the format apart from the others in this repository.

schemaVersion.title: Schema version
schemaVersion.description: The version of this format the record follows. Each version of the schema accepts only its own version string, so a record never silently passes against a schema it wasn't written for.

id.description: This report's identifier, unique within the system that created it, such as the incident reporting system's event number.

externalIds.title: External identifiers
externalIds.description: Ids for this report in other systems: the incident reporting tool, a patient safety organization (PSO) submission, risk management or a state reporting portal.

createdAt.description: When the record was created in the system that holds it. The report's own time is reporter.reportedAt.

updatedAt.description: When the record was last changed.

facility.title: Facility
facility.description: The facility where the event happened. A small facility plus an event date can identify a patient, which is one reason records remain confidential.

id.description: The facility's id in the system the report comes from.

type.title: Facility type
type.description: The kind of facility: hospital; ambulatory-surgery-center; clinic (physician office, outpatient clinic); long-term-care (skilled nursing, nursing home, assisted living); behavioral-health; pharmacy (community or outpatient pharmacy); home-health; emergency-medical-services; or other. The AHRQ Common Formats have separate versions for hospitals, community pharmacies and skilled nursing facilities; this field records the setting either way.

identifiers.title: Identifiers
identifiers.description: Facility identifiers, such as the CMS Certification Number (scheme CCN), a National Provider Identifier (scheme NPI) or a state license number. These identify the facility, not the patient.

jurisdiction.description: Where the facility is licensed and regulated, which decides what must be reported and to whom.

event.title: Event
event.description: When and where the event happened and when it was found. The gap between occurredAt and discoveredAt is itself a safety measure (time to detection).

occurredAt.description: When the event happened, with the UTC offset in effect at the facility. Leave out if unknown; set occurredAtPrecision to say how sure the time is.

occurredAtPrecision.title: Occurrence time precision
occurredAtPrecision.description: How exact occurredAt is: exact (observed or recorded at the time), approximate (estimated afterwards, for example an unwitnessed fall) or unknown (occurredAt is a placeholder or left out).

discoveredAt.description: When staff discovered the event. Required, because every report has a discovery time even when the event time is unknown. Must not be before occurredAt.

location.title: Location
location.description: Where in the facility the event happened. Keep it to what trending needs: a room number with a date can identify a patient.

type.title: Location type
type.description: The kind of area: inpatient-unit, intensive-care, emergency-department, operating-room, procedure-area (endoscopy, cath lab, interventional radiology), labor-and-delivery, outpatient-area, pharmacy, laboratory, imaging, patient-home (for home health), transport (between areas or facilities), common-area (hallways, lobbies, grounds) or other.

unit.title: Unit
unit.description: The unit or department name as the facility uses it.

detail.title: Detail
detail.description: A more precise place, when it matters to the analysis (for example patient bathroom, medication room). Avoid room or bed numbers in records shared outside the facility.

eventType.title: Event type
eventType.description: What kind of patient safety event this is, using the three event types of the AHRQ Common Formats. incident: an event that reached the patient, whether or not the patient was harmed (ICPS splits these into no-harm incidents and harmful incidents, or adverse events). near-miss: an event that did not reach the patient, also called a close call (the ICPS near miss). unsafe-condition: any circumstance that increases the probability of a patient safety event, and that does not involve an identifiable patient (the ICPS reportable circumstance). The validator checks reachedPatient, harm and patient agree with the type.

eventCategory.title: Event category
eventCategory.description: The clinical area of the event, following the event categories of the AHRQ Common Formats for Event Reporting – Hospital: blood-or-blood-product; device-or-medical-supply (AHRQ: Device or Medical/Surgical Supply, including Health Information Technology); fall; healthcare-associated-infection; medication-or-other-substance; perinatal; pressure-injury (Pressure Ulcer in Common Formats versions 1.1 and 1.2); surgery-or-anesthesia (includes invasive procedures); venous-thromboembolism; or other, for events outside these categories (describe them with eventSubcategory). Pick the category the event is about, not every category it touches; use contributingFactors for the rest.

eventSubcategory.title: Event subcategory
eventSubcategory.description: A finer classification in the reporting organization's own taxonomy, for trending within the category.

description.title: Description
description.description: What happened, in the reporter's words: the sequence of events, what was found and what was done. Don't include patient names, dates of birth, record numbers, addresses or other direct identifiers; refer to 'the patient'. The schema can't enforce that, so screen this field before sharing a record outside the organization.

patient.title: Patient
patient.description: Facts about the patient involved that analysis needs and that can't identify the patient on their own. The object is closed (additionalProperties is false), so names, dates of birth, medical record numbers, addresses and the like are rejected rather than stored. Leave the whole block out for an unsafe condition, which by definition involves no identifiable patient.

ageBand.title: Age band
ageBand.description: The patient's age at the time of the event, as a band rather than a date of birth (a date of birth is a direct identifier). The bands are those of the AHRQ Common Formats (version 1.1) patient information form: neonate (0 to 28 days), infant (more than 28 days and under 1 year), child (1 to 12 years), adolescent (13 to 17), adult-18-64, adult-65-74, adult-75-84, adult-85-plus, or unknown.

sex.title: Sex
sex.description: The patient's sex as recorded in the source system: female, male, other, or unknown (not recorded or not disclosed).

encounterRef.title: Encounter reference
encounterRef.description: An opaque key that lets authorized staff find the encounter in the source system. It must be a surrogate (a random token kept in a lookup table that stays inside the organization), not the medical record number, account number or visit number, because those are direct identifiers under HIPAA. With the lookup table, this key re-identifies the patient, so don't share it outside the organization.

reachedPatient.title: Reached the patient
reachedPatient.description: Whether the event reached the patient. true for an incident, false for a near miss; leave out for an unsafe condition. Recording it separately from eventType lets the validator catch a misclassified report.

harm.title: Harm
harm.description: The assessed harm to the patient, for events that reached the patient (incidents) only. The levels follow the AHRQ Common Formats Harm Scale (version 1.2): harm remaining after the event was discovered and any attempts to reduce its consequences, assessed at a stated time. Near misses and unsafe conditions have no harm block; the validator checks this.

level.title: Harm level
level.description: death: the patient died, and the event caused or brought forward the death. severe-harm: bodily or psychological injury, including pain or disfigurement, that interferes significantly with functional ability or quality of life. moderate-harm: bodily or psychological injury that adversely affects functional ability or quality of life, but not at the level of severe harm. mild-harm: minimal symptoms or loss of function, or injury limited to additional treatment, monitoring or a longer stay. no-harm: the event reached the patient, but no harm was evident. unknown: harm can't be assessed yet; update the record when it can.

duration.title: Duration
duration.description: For mild, moderate or severe harm, whether it is expected to be permanent (lifelong) or temporary, at the time of assessment; unknown when the prognosis isn't clear yet.

additionalTreatment.title: Additional treatment
additionalTreatment.description: Whether the patient needed additional treatment, monitoring or a longer stay because of the event. Recorded separately because it drives cost and is often known before the final harm level.

assessedAt.description: When harm was assessed. The harm level is a prognosis at this time and can change; reassess and update the record (the audit trail keeps the earlier value).

assessedBy.description: Who assessed harm, usually a clinician or the patient safety officer.

contributingFactors.title: Contributing factors
contributingFactors.description: Circumstances that contributed to the event, as many as apply. This list is this format's own, chosen for the factors safety teams most often trend; it maps onto the WHO ICPS contributing factor groups (staff, patient, work environment, organizational and service, external) but is not either framework's list.

items.title: Contributing factor
items.description: One contributing factor and how it contributed.

category.title: Category
category.description: communication (between staff, or with the patient or family); handoff (transfer of care or information between people or units); staffing (numbers or skill mix); training (knowledge or competence); policy-or-procedure (missing, unclear or not followed); equipment-or-device (failure, design or use); environment (layout, lighting, noise, clutter); patient-factors (condition, behavior, language, adherence); task-factors (complexity, interruptions, time pressure); team-factors (supervision, roles, teamwork); organizational-culture (reporting culture, normalized deviance, priorities); labeling-or-packaging (look-alike or sound-alike products, unclear labels); information-system (EHR, order entry or other IT design or failure); other.

detail.title: Detail
detail.description: How this factor contributed, specifically enough that someone could act on it.

immediateActions.title: Immediate actions
immediateActions.description: What was done straight away to care for the patient and make the situation safe, before any investigation. Corrective actions to prevent recurrence go in investigation.actions.

takenByRole.title: Taken by (role)
takenByRole.description: The role of the person who acted, rather than their name: roles are what analysis needs, and names of staff in safety reports are sensitive.

reporter.title: Reporter
reporter.description: Who reported the event. Reporting systems commonly allow anonymous reports, because people report more when they can't be blamed. An anonymous report has no contact details (the schema rejects them), and the validator also checks that the submission entries in statusHistory and auditTrail don't name the reporter. Even then, role plus unit can identify someone on a small team; systems should consider that before showing role to wide audiences.

anonymous.title: Anonymous
anonymous.description: Whether the reporter chose to stay anonymous. When true, contact must be left out.

role.title: Role
role.description: The reporter's role: physician; advanced-practice-provider (nurse practitioner, physician assistant, nurse anesthetist, nurse midwife); nurse; pharmacist; other-clinician (therapist, technologist, other licensed clinical staff); non-clinical-staff; patient-or-family; or other.

contact.description: How to reach the reporter for follow-up questions or feedback. Not allowed when the report is anonymous.

reportedAt.description: When the report was made. Must not be before event.discoveredAt.

wantsFeedback.title: Wants feedback
wantsFeedback.description: Whether the reporter asked to hear what came of the report. Closing the loop with reporters is a mark of a working reporting culture, so systems should track it.

notifications.title: Notifications
notifications.description: Who was told about the event, when and how: the patient or family (disclosure), clinicians and leaders, and outside bodies such as a state agency, an accreditor, a patient safety organization or a device manufacturer. Recording whether a rule required each notification makes missed or late mandatory reports visible.

recipient.title: Recipient
recipient.description: Who was notified: patient-or-family; attending-clinician; unit-leadership; risk-management; patient-safety-officer; regulatory-agency (for example a state health department); patient-safety-organization (a PSO); accreditation-body; manufacturer (for example under a device reporting program); insurer; or other.

recipientName.title: Recipient name
recipientName.description: The named agency or body, where it matters which one. For patient-or-family, leave this out rather than naming the person.

method.title: Method
method.description: How: in-person, phone, letter, email, portal (a reporting portal or patient portal) or other.

requiredByRule.title: Required by rule
requiredByRule.description: Whether a law, regulation, accreditation standard or internal policy required this notification.

ruleReference.title: Rule reference
ruleReference.description: The rule that required it, as cited locally.

reference.title: Reference
reference.description: A confirmation, case or report number the recipient gave.

investigation.title: Investigation
investigation.description: The review of why the event happened and what will change. Many organizations investigate only some events (for example by harm level); leave this out until an investigation starts.

method.title: Method
method.description: How the event was analyzed: root-cause-analysis (a full systems analysis, as used for sentinel events); apparent-cause-analysis (a more limited review, usually for lower-harm events); failure-mode-and-effects-analysis (a prospective analysis of a process, sometimes triggered by an event); case-review (peer or clinical case review); or none (reviewed and closed without a formal analysis).

completedAt.description: When the investigation was completed. Must not be before startedAt.

summary.title: Summary
summary.description: What the investigation found, in a few paragraphs.

causes.title: Causes
causes.description: The root or apparent causes identified, one per entry, written as system causes rather than individual blame.

actions.title: Action plan
actions.description: The action plan: changes to prevent recurrence, each with its strength, owner, due date and measure.

strength.title: Strength
strength.description: How strong the action is, on the action hierarchy used in root cause analysis (developed by the US Department of Veterans Affairs National Center for Patient Safety and used in RCA²): stronger actions change the system so the error is hard to make (forcing functions, standardized equipment, removing hazards); intermediate actions make errors less likely or easier to catch (checklists, redundancy, software enhancements); weaker actions rely on people remembering (training, new policy, warnings). Action plans made only of weaker actions rarely prevent recurrence.

owner.description: Who is responsible for completing the action.

status.title: Status
status.description: planned, in-progress, complete or cancelled (with the reason in the audit trail).

measure.title: Measure of success
measure.description: How the organization will know the action worked: a measurable check, not 'staff educated'.
examples: Monthly audit of 20 beds finds no alarms below minimum volume.

psoSubmission.title: PSO submission
psoSubmission.description: Submission of the report to a patient safety organization (PSO), where the organization works with one. In the US, information reported to a PSO can be patient safety work product with privilege and confidentiality protections under the Patient Safety and Quality Improvement Act; this field records the submission and doesn't decide that question.

submitted.title: Submitted
submitted.description: Whether the report was submitted to the PSO.

commonFormatsVersion.title: Common Formats version
commonFormatsVersion.description: The version of the AHRQ Common Formats the submission used, as the PSO names it.

status.description: Where the report is in its review: submitted (received, not yet looked at); triaged (classified and assigned); under-investigation; action-plan (investigation done, corrective actions in progress); closed; or not-a-safety-event (reviewed and found not to be a patient safety event, for example a pure facilities issue).

statusHistory.title: Status history
statusHistory.description: Every status the report has had, oldest first, ending at the current status (the validator checks both). For an anonymous report, leave by out of the submission entry.

status.description: The status the record moved to, one of this format's status values.

attachments.title: Attachments
attachments.description: Files that belong to the report, such as an investigation report or a photograph of a device. Keep identifiable clinical documents in the clinical record, not here.

auditTrail.title: Audit trail
auditTrail.description: Recorded actions on the report, oldest first. For an anonymous report, don't record the reporter as the actor who created or submitted it.

extensions.description: Local fields this format doesn't define, namespaced as <namespace>:<field>. Don't use extensions to add patient identifiers the format deliberately leaves out.

status.title: Status
status.description: The status values of this format, defined once so status and statusHistory use the same list. Where the report is in its review: submitted (received, not yet looked at); triaged (classified and assigned); under-investigation; action-plan (investigation done, corrective actions in progress); closed; or not-a-safety-event (reviewed and found not to be a patient safety event, for example a pure facilities issue).
